The passage explores urban alienation and precarious security by following a man’s dizzying perception from a high-rise apartment window, blending fragmented description with sensory and commercial details. It reveals that the apartment’s promised order and desirability mask an unstable, swamp-like reality below, suggesting that modern comfort rests on fragile and unsettling foundations.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: He walked to

outputs.L1: He walked to the window and stared down twenty stories to the street, gaseous and dizzy as a swamp—not visible from this height, though there had been a street down there, and he knew it. It came with the apartment, with the guarded foyers and halls, the doorman holstered beneath his uniform, and the television split-screening the front and rear entrances. He knew it was all there, and he was here, twenty stories above the unsettled swamp-mist. He knew the trucks bound for the bridge were still passing nearby; he could feel them rumbling through the soles of his feet. So he knew the floor he walked on was someone’s ceiling, and it was all normal tonight and countable: a two-year lease, because a desirable apartment with a full view of the river—a five-by-three balcony through the door—required a $200 deposit; fully carpeted; self-defrosting refrigerator. The balcony door was stuck, but he could stare twenty stories down from the windowsill, watching the swamp-smoke curl and thin, the swamp lapping at the base, and the unpaid-for miracle rising one inch at a time.
outputs.L2:
He went over to the window and looked down from the twentieth floor toward the street, which from that height seemed vaporous, unsteady, swamp-like, and almost impossible to see. Still, he knew a street existed below. It was part of the place: the apartment, the protected lobbies and corridors, the doorman with a holster hidden under his uniform, and the television monitor showing both the front and back entrances at once.

He knew all of it was there, and that he was up here, twenty floors above the restless swamp-fog. He also knew the trucks heading for the bridge were still going by nearby; he could sense their vibration through the bottoms of his feet. That meant the floor beneath him was also someone else’s ceiling. Everything tonight was ordinary and measurable: a two-year lease; a desirable unit with a complete river view; a five-by-three balcony beyond the door; a $200 deposit; wall-to-wall carpeting; a self-defrosting refrigerator. The balcony door would not open, but he could still look down from the windowsill, twenty stories above, watching the swampy vapors coil and fade, the swamp washing against the building’s base, and the not-yet-paid-for miracle advancing inch by inch.
outputs.L3:
He stands at the window of a twentieth-floor apartment, looking out toward a street he cannot clearly see. It is far below him, hidden by mist, yet he remains intensely aware of its presence. The distance should make him feel removed from it, protected by height and glass, but instead the obscured street seems to press upward into his thoughts.

The apartment itself appears secure, ordinary, and thoroughly accounted for. It is part of a managed building with guarded entrances, a doorman, surveillance, and all the formal assurances of a lease. Everything about it suggests safety and legitimacy: access is controlled, the residents are watched over, and the space has been purchased or rented according to the proper rules of urban life.

Around him, the city continues to move. Even though the view is blurred, he can sense traffic nearby, especially in the low rumble of trucks passing through the streets. Their sound confirms that the world outside has not disappeared; it is still operating beyond the mist, heavy and mechanical, surrounding the apartment building on all sides.

The narrator also draws attention to the apartment’s advertised comforts. It has a river view, a balcony, carpeting, and a refrigerator—features that belong to the language of real estate brochures and middle-class convenience. These details make the apartment seem desirable and normal, a place meant to offer comfort, status, and security high above the city.

Yet beneath these ordinary details, the scene feels unstable and uncanny. The mist does not simply hide the street; it seems almost swamp-like, as if it were rising around the building and threatening to engulf it. The apartment’s modern security and domestic comforts cannot fully dispel this atmosphere. Instead, they make the unease sharper: behind the familiar surfaces of urban life, something damp, obscure, and unsettling appears to be gathering.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents a vivid exploration of urban alienation and the fragile sense of security offered by modern city living. It follows a man as he looks out from the window of a high-rise apartment, allowing his perception to become dizzying, fragmented, and unstable. From this elevated position, the city appears both organized and disorienting: streets, buildings, advertisements, lights, and distant movements form a broken collage of impressions. The description blends physical sensations with commercial details, suggesting that the modern urban environment is not experienced as a coherent whole but as a series of disconnected images, sounds, and signs. The man’s viewpoint emphasizes his separation from the world below, making the apartment seem less like a place of comfort than a suspended and isolating space.

At first, the apartment may appear to represent order, desirability, and protection. Its height, design, and association with modern convenience suggest safety and success. Yet the passage gradually undermines this promise. Beneath the polished surface of the building and the controlled image of urban comfort lies something unstable and unsettling. The ground below is imagined almost like a swamp, a place of hidden movement, uncertainty, and decay. This contrast between the apartment’s marketed appeal and the threatening reality beneath it reveals the precariousness of the man’s security. What seems solid and desirable is shown to depend on fragile foundations.

Through this contrast, the passage suggests a broader criticism of modern urban life. The city offers comfort, status, and the illusion of order, but these benefits are haunted by anxiety and instability. The man’s disoriented perception reflects a deeper unease: he is physically sheltered, yet psychologically unsettled; elevated above the city, yet unable to feel truly secure. In this way, the passage shows that modern comfort is not as stable as it appears. It rests on uncertain ground, masking a world that remains chaotic, alienating, and disturbingly fragile.
outputs.L5:
He walked to the edge of the quiet street, where the morning light spilled across the pavement like gold. The world was still waking up: windows opened, birds called from rooftops, and the scent of fresh bread drifted from a nearby bakery.

He walked to the old wooden bench beneath the chestnut tree and sat down for a moment, listening to the city breathe. In his pocket was a letter he had read a dozen times, its words folded into his thoughts. Today was the day he would finally answer it.

After a deep breath, he stood again. He walked to the station with steady steps, no longer afraid of what waited ahead. Each step carried him closer to a new beginning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single long, breathless paragraph in the style of postmodern literary fiction about a man in a high-rise apartment looking down at a city street that seems to turn into a swamp, blending real-estate language with paranoia and urban unease.
counterfactuals.output: From the forty-seventh floor, in what the brochure had called an elevated sanctuary of glass, steel, and curated silence, he stood barefoot on the engineered oak and looked down through the floor-to-ceiling windows at the street, or what had until recently been the street, because at dusk the traffic lanes had begun to darken and pulse and lose their municipal certainty, the asphalt softening into a black-green sheen like old water under a skin of oil, the crosswalks sagging into pale reeds, the median strips widening, breathing, exhaling mosquito-colored shadows, and the cars—those leased, financed, insured units of private velocity—seemed less parked than stranded, half-submerged among the glimmering humps of curb and hydrant, while the building’s marketing language returned to him with the force of an accusation: unobstructed views, premium adjacency, a rare vertical lifestyle opportunity, as if height could absolve him from whatever was rising down there, as if the concierge lobby with its stone waterfall wall and scent-diffused air and triple-secured access points were not merely a polished throat through which the swamp had already begun to speak; he pressed his forehead to the chilled pane and watched a bus kneel at the corner and not rise again, watched pedestrians hesitate at the edge of a puddle that elongated into a channel, watched umbrellas bloom like fungi and drift apart, each person suddenly reduced to a speck of indecision in a landscape whose zoning had been revoked by some older, wetter authority, and he wondered whether the city had always been this, a marsh with mortgages, a fever dream subdivided into parcels, the towers driven down like stakes into mud that remembered everything—the buried creeks, the filled-in coves, the demolished tenements, the hands that signed, stamped, evicted, acquired, leveraged, flipped—while above him the recessed lights hummed with the white confidence of model units and quarterly reports; somewhere behind the walls the pipes ticked, the ventilation whispered, the smart thermostat adjusted itself with obscene discretion, and he imagined the entire condominium association listening through the drywall, the board president in 51B, the silent couple in 44F, the investor who never visited but owned six units under different shell companies, all of them waiting for him to admit what he could see: that the street signs were leaning like drowned crosses, that steam was coming from the manholes in slow reptilian gusts, that the traffic signal blinked red into the vapor with the dumb persistence of a warning no one had budgeted to receive, and that beneath the glamorous amenity deck, beneath the co-working lounge and pet spa and residents-only wine storage, something soft and toothless and patient was swallowing the value of everything one inch at a time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal prose passage where someone stands twenty stories up in a guarded luxury apartment, sensing trucks, bridges, doormen, television monitors, and the street below dissolving into mist and swamp water.
counterfactuals.output:
Twenty stories up, in the guarded hush of the luxury apartment, she stood barefoot before the glass and felt the building pretend to be solid.

Below, the doormen remained at their posts in their green coats and polished shoes, but their faces had begun to blur on the television monitors in the lobby, the screens blooming with static like frost on a pond. Each monitor showed a different entrance, a different angle of marble, brass, revolving door, umbrella stand—yet all of them were slowly filling with the same pale vapor. Trucks moved along the avenue with their headlights on, enormous and patient, but the sound of their engines arrived late, softened, as if driven through blankets of wet moss.

Farther out, the bridges had lost their steel. Their cables drooped into the air like vines, their towers fading until they seemed less built than remembered. Traffic crossed them anyway, red taillights drifting in procession over nothing. The city’s grid loosened. Corners rounded themselves. Pavement darkened, buckled, and took on the sheen of water.

She pressed her palm to the window. It was cold, then damp.

The street below dissolved by degrees: first the painted lines, then the curbs, then the black mouths of storm drains. Mist rose from the crosswalks. Swamp water gathered where taxis had been, spreading in slow green mirrors around the ankles of pedestrians who did not look down. The awning over the entrance sagged with reeds. The doormen lifted their white-gloved hands to greet residents arriving from a street that was no longer a street, only a channel of murky water carrying newspapers, lilies, and the faint glow of submerged traffic signals.

In the apartment behind her, the furniture held its expensive poses. Lamps shone. A bowl of fruit gleamed as though waxed for an afterlife. But from the vents came the smell of mud, and on every muted television monitor the same image flickered: the building floating alone, tall and lit, while the world around it breathed, sank, and returned to something older than roads.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I need an experimental fiction excerpt with no normal sentence boundaries: a tenant at a window in a high-rise reflects on the lease, balcony, appliances, security, and a strange rising swamp beneath the building.
counterfactuals.output:
from the forty-third floor the lease looks thinner than it did in the office, a pale legal skin held up to the window, clauses breathing whenever the elevator cables hum, tenant agrees, tenant acknowledges, tenant shall not keep birds or dismantle smoke detectors or interfere with the quiet enjoyment of other tenants, and I press my thumb against the glass where the balcony begins beyond the locked sliding door, not a balcony really but a shelf for weather, a concrete tongue with a drain in its mouth and a railing that trembles when the wind reads it aloud

below, the city has been losing its edges

at first it was only water in the service alley, black and reflective, a municipal oversight, then reeds appeared around the loading dock, then insects struck the lobby lights with soft grammatical insistence, then the superintendent sent a notice about temporary moisture events, then the moisture learned to stand upright, green-backed, patient, shouldering aside the dumpsters, lifting the parked cars by their axles as if examining them for ripeness

the refrigerator clicks behind me like a small landlord approving something, the stove’s digital clock blinks twelve twelve twelve though I have set it every morning, the dishwasher fills itself at night and steams without dishes, the washing machine turns one sock for hours in ceremonial water, all appliances included in rent, all repairs to be requested through the portal, emergency requests defined as fire, flood, loss of heat, active intrusion, but what is intrusion if the swamp has always been here under the foundation, if the building was only a temporary opinion poured into pilings

security called yesterday to say my guest privileges had been suspended because the cameras had seen movement on my balcony, though no one can reach it without passing through my unit or falling from the roof, I said perhaps it was a heron, they said residents are responsible for all visitors, I said perhaps it was the reflection of a heron, they said reflections must be registered after ten p.m., I said perhaps it was the lease itself trying to leave, dragging its staples across the tile, looking for softer ground

now the lobby turnstiles are submerged to the waist, still blinking green, green, green beneath the brown water, accepting key fobs from fish, the concierge desk floats diagonally against the mailroom door, and the intercom crackles with a voice from somewhere below, not drowning exactly, more like germinating, reminding us that balconies are not to be used for storage, that towels may not be hung from railings, that no alterations may be made to exterior appearances, including vines, nests, prayer flags, distress signals, or roots

I unlock the sliding door despite the addendum, despite the wind, despite the security camera swiveling toward me with its single wet eye, and the balcony exhales heat from the swamp rising floor by floor, carrying the smell of pennies, orchids, basement carpet, old signatures, something ancient and leased month to month

the building sways

in the glass I see myself multiplied in all the dark apartments across the shaft, each tenant holding a page, each page blooming mildew at the margins, each mouth moving around the same clause, surrender of premises, surrender of premises, surrender, while below us the swamp lifts one patient hand to take possession, not of the tower, not yet, but of its reflection first, pulling the whole lit column down into its trembling duplicate where the elevators descend forever and every button is marked ground
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense Don DeLillo-esque paragraph about urban alienation in an apartment tower, including details like a doorman, split-screen security TV, a river view, a stuck balcony door, and a street far below becoming swamp-like.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Don DeLillo’s exact style, but here’s an original paragraph with a cool, paranoid, postmodern tone and urban alienation:

The tower stood in its own weather of glass, sealed apartments stacked above the avenue like evidence files, each window lit by a different insomnia. In the lobby the doorman watched the split-screen security TV with the remote sorrow of a man monitoring distant wars: elevator, mailroom, service corridor, curbside blur. Upstairs, the river view arrived flattened and metallic, a strip of moving gray beyond the furniture, beyond the hum of climate control, while the balcony door remained stuck in its track, resisting weather, breath, accident, any proof that the city still entered the room. Far below, the street lost its edges in the rain, taxis nosing through black water, pedestrians shrinking under plastic hoods, the crosswalks dissolving into something marshy and ancestral, as if the grid itself were remembering swamp, and everyone in the tower—tenant, guest, courier, watcher—felt the same mute pressure of height, the old fear of being seen and not known.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness scene in which a man looks down from his twentieth-floor apartment and tries to reassure himself everything is normal while the city below feels gaseous, unstable, and slowly flooding.
counterfactuals.output:
He told himself it was only weather.

Weather did this. Heat did this. Rain coming in from the river, pressure falling, the glass sweating in its frame, the city loosening at the edges the way things did in August. There was nothing in it. Nothing to make a person stand barefoot at the window of a twentieth-floor apartment at 3:17 in the afternoon with one hand on the sill and the other pressed flat against his own chest, as if keeping something from opening there.

Everything was normal.

The traffic still moved on Hart Street, although it moved strangely, not in lanes so much as in slow dark threads, headlights smeared even though it was day. Buses sighed at the stops. A woman under a red umbrella waited at the corner, or something red did. The awning of the pharmacy bellied and snapped. Steam rose from the manhole covers, but steam always rose from manhole covers, that was practically the city’s signature, its little theatrical habit, proof of warmth below, pipes below, industry, maintenance, men in helmets drinking coffee in tunnels and saying ordinary obscene things to one another. A functioning city had vapors.

A city breathed.

He tried to say that out loud and found he had only mouthed it. His reflection mouthed it back to him in the window: a gray man in a white undershirt, needing a shave, needing sleep, needing not to read the news before breakfast or after breakfast or during lunch or in bed. Behind the reflection, the towers across the avenue wavered as if seen through boiling water. Their edges dissolved, recovered, dissolved again. One office building seemed to lean minutely, not physically, not enough for an engineer to care, but in intention, in mood. It had lost confidence in verticality.

Optical effect, he thought.

Rain on the glass.

But the rain had not started.

Below, at the intersection, the crosswalk stripes shone with a thin reflective film. It pooled first in the gutters, a silver trembling line along the curb, then breathed outward over the asphalt. He watched the water make islands of the trash bags waiting for collection. Black plastic domes, tied shut, glossy and patient. A delivery cyclist lifted both feet from his pedals and coasted through a shallow sheet of it, leaving a V-shaped wake.

Normal, the man thought again, though he did not like the wake. He did not like that the wake remained after the bicycle had gone, spreading and spreading, widening into the street with no apparent source.

The sink, he remembered suddenly.

He turned from the window. The apartment was exactly as it had been. Sofa, table, cup with the brown ring of morning coffee. A book open facedown like a small animal pretending not to be dead. The kitchen light humming. No sound of running water. No flooded floor. No catastrophic pipe burst, no domestic explanation he could seize by the neck.

He went to the sink anyway and turned the tap. Water came out obediently, clear and narrow, striking the basin with a domestic sound so intimate it embarrassed him. He turned it off. A final drop swelled at the faucet, hung there, fat with decision, then fell.

See?

He almost laughed. He had become the sort of person who checked a faucet because the street below looked wet.

But when he returned to the window the city had softened further. The lower floors of the opposite buildings were blurred, not hidden exactly, but diluted. Storefront signs glowed in halos. The green cross of the pharmacy pulsed in the vapors, larger than it should have been, a medical moon. Cars on Hart Street pushed through water now deep enough to cover their tires halfway. Their engines made muted animal noises. At the corner the red umbrella had tipped, become a red petal floating away.

No, he thought. No, I’m misjudging distance. Twentieth floor. Perspective. Refraction. There are words for this.

He began naming what he could see, because naming had always helped. Lamppost. Newsstand. Bus shelter. Maple tree. One taxi, two taxis. The old hotel with the green cornice. The white van double-parked in front of the bakery. The bakery, of course, open, lights on, someone inside moving behind the steamed window. Flour on a counter. Trays. Bread. If bread was being made, if someone was scoring dough with a blade and sliding it into an oven, then the day had not left its rails.

The streetlights flickered on.

It was afternoon.

Clouds hung low between the buildings, except clouds did not hang between buildings like laundry. Fog, then. River fog. A marine layer. The city was on an estuary; this was in the guidebooks, in the weather apps, in the damp swollen doors of old apartments. Fog came in and made liars of distances. It muffled sirens. It made everything cinematic and inconvenient. It did not mean anything.

He pressed his forehead to the window. The glass was cold now. Under his skin, his pulse answered.

Somewhere below, a horn sounded and did not stop. Not a car horn, not exactly. It began as one note and widened, joined by others, a mass complaint rising from the avenues. He looked for the source but the streets were becoming indistinct, vehicles reduced to slow luminous organs moving under a membrane. The water had taken the sidewalks. It climbed the first steps of the bank. It accepted newspapers, cups, a single shoe, the orange cones around a construction pit. The cones bobbed solemnly, as if marking a hazard no longer special enough to matter.

He laughed then, one short puff, because the cones looked stupid.

Good. That was good. If something could still look stupid, the world had not ended. The end of the world would be majestic, surely, or loud, or at least decisive. Not this soft confusion, this embarrassing seepage, this city losing form like a cough held too long in the lungs.

Gaseous, he thought, and hated the word because it was right.

The avenues exhaled. Vapor leaked from grates and basement doors, from subway entrances, from the seams between buildings. It did not rise cleanly but billowed sideways, shouldered by the wind, folding through the streets in yellow-gray masses. The tops of cars disappeared first, then reappeared in pieces: roof, windshield, roof again. Pedestrians became dark upright strokes and then smudges. The city below was no longer built of stone and steel and glass but of densities, pressures, uncertain thicknesses. Even sound seemed to arrive in bubbles.

He looked up, away from the street, toward the higher floors across the avenue. People stood at windows. That should have comforted him. It did, for a second. Here was proof: others seeing what he saw, others pausing mid-email, mid-shower, mid-argument, coming to the glass with wet hair or shirtsleeves rolled. A child pressed both hands to a pane. An old man in suspenders leaned forward through curtains. On the roof of the building opposite, pigeons lifted all at once, circled, and settled again, as if embarrassed by panic.

Everything is normal, he told the strangers. We are all simply looking.

His phone buzzed on the table.

He did not want to check it because checking it would either confirm something or fail to, and both possibilities seemed unbearable. If there was an alert, then the thing had a name. If there was no alert, then the thing was nameless and belonged more intimately to him.

It buzzed again.

Probably his sister. Probably a delivery notification. Probably some cheerful automated reminder that his dentist appointment had been rescheduled. His teeth, he thought. In the middle of all this, his teeth still existed, still needed cleaning. The persistence of appointments was another argument for normalcy.

He picked up the phone.

No signal.

That happened. On the twentieth floor, inexplicably, it happened. Elevators, storms, overloaded towers. He set the phone down gently, as though not startling it.

The building groaned.

Buildings groaned. Pipes knocked. Ducts flexed. Neighbors dragged furniture with the mysterious devotion of neighbors everywhere. He listened hard and identified, or tried to identify, the ordinary components of the sound: elevator cable, plumbing, wind shear, old concrete settling into its own age. Nothing catastrophic. Nothing alive.

Then the lights flickered, not off, only dimmer, then full again.

He went to the door and opened it.

The hallway smelled of wet carpet and onions. Mrs. Alvarez from 20C was there in her slippers, holding a saucepan. Why a saucepan? She looked at him and then past him toward his windows.

“Do you see it?” she asked.

He nearly said no.

The word rose in him automatically, polite and treacherous. No, nothing, probably weather. No, I was just making coffee. No, I haven’t been standing at the glass for twenty minutes watching the city lose its outline.

Instead he said, “It’s rain.”

“It isn’t raining.”

“It will,” he said.

She looked down at her saucepan as if surprised to find it in her hands. From the stairwell came voices, ascending or descending, impossible to tell. A child crying. A man saying, “Don’t use the elevator,” in a tone of artificial calm so similar to his own thoughts that he disliked him immediately.

Mrs. Alvarez said, “My son is at school.”

Schools were normal. Attendance sheets, crayons, bad lunches in partitioned trays. He saw, with a force that made him grip the doorframe, a classroom on the fourth floor of some municipal building, bright cut-out letters on the wall, twenty small backpacks hanging from hooks while water climbed the stairwell step by step.

“They’ll have plans,” he said. “They have procedures.”

“Yes,” she said, and did not move.

They stood like that until another groan passed through the building, deeper this time, or perhaps lower, as though the foundation had cleared its throat.

He closed the door more quickly than he intended.

At the window, the water had reached the traffic lights. Or no, impossible. He blinked. The signal heads still hung above the intersection, changing from red to green to yellow with professional indifference, but the poles vanished halfway down into vapor and reflected flood, so they looked rooted in nothing. A bus drifted sideways against a row of parked cars. Its interior lights glowed. No passengers visible. Maybe evacuated. Maybe simply obscured.

The city’s surfaces were separating from one another. Reflections no longer matched their objects. The glass towers lengthened downward into the water, deeper than the buildings were tall. Streets he knew by heart bent away from their usual directions. Hart Street seemed to run north now, or down, or inward. He could not keep the map in his head from becoming a wet paper thing.

He backed away, sat on the sofa, stood again.

Normal men did not pace. Or they did; they paced while waiting for test results, while on hold with insurance companies, while deciding whether to apologize. Pacing was not evidence.

He tried the television. Blue screen, then a frozen image of a cooking show: a woman smiling over a bowl of lemons. Her mouth was open around a word she would never finish. He turned it off.

The apartment had become very quiet.

Not silent; silence would have been dramatic. Quiet. The refrigerator’s tick, the little electrical whine of the router, the distant plumbing shudder. His own breathing, too loud and too wet. He swallowed and tasted metal.

He thought of all the things below him that had basements. Restaurants with sacks of rice on shelves. Laundry rooms. Boiler rooms. Wine cellars. The subway tunnels under Hart, tiled in white, maps peeling under glass, rats made buoyant and indignant. He imagined the water finding every descent, every stair, every forgotten door, entering without malice. That was worst: no malice. The flood did not hate the city. The vapor did not intend to erase it. They were only obeying gradient, pressure, gravity, laws older and calmer than zoning.

He returned to the window because not looking was worse.

Now the lower half of the city was gone.

Above the fog-flood, towers rose like unfinished thoughts. Sirens flashed under the surface in red pulses. A helicopter moved between buildings and vanished behind a curtain of vapor. The roof garden on the building opposite shed leaves into the air, and the leaves did not fall so much as hover, spin, and descend reluctantly into the gray.

He placed both palms against the glass.

“Everything is normal,” he said.

His voice sounded ridiculous, but also brave, in the limited way ridiculous things can be brave. He said it again for practice, for rhythm, for the molecules in the room.

“Everything is normal.”

Behind him, in the kitchen, the drain gurgled.

He did not turn around.

The window trembled gently under his hands. Far below, or not far enough, something large struck something larger with a dull aquatic boom. The city exhaled, and the vapor rose another floor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
